title: Does The Tantrum Help?
author: The Daily Stoic
summary: This short Daily Stoic meditation confronts the reflex to rage when fortune delivers the unexpected, from travel delays to embezzling employees. It asks a blunt series of questions about whether yelling, spiraling, or assigning blame ever changes the outcome. The piece turns on a pointed parallel with parenting: adults tell children that tantrums do not work, are a bad look, and are no longer age appropriate, yet indulge the same behavior at airline counters, in rude emails, and on social media. Borrowing a Phoebe Bridgers lyric about throwing a tantrum when things are not as imagined, it frames the adult outburst as the same childish move. The conclusion is characteristically Stoic and practical: accept what happened and redirect energy into the work that can actually make a difference.
points: Fortune, in the Stoic view, behaves as she pleases, so disruptions that are not our fault should be expected rather than treated as outrages.
The rules adults enforce on children about tantrums apply equally to adult outbursts at service workers, in email, and online.
Blame and venting offer only a few minutes of relief and change nothing about the underlying problem.
The only productive response to an unwelcome event is to get back to work on what can still be done.
quotes: Things happen—things that are not our fault, things we didn’t expect, things that are going to cause problems. From travel delays to embezzling employees, from world events to family drama, fortune behaves as she pleases, the Stoics tell us.
But what does getting upset about this do? Does yelling and screaming change anything? Does spiraling fix it? Does finding someone to blame make you feel better for more than a few minutes?
You tell your children that it doesn’t. You tell them that it doesn’t get them what they want. You tell them that it’s a bad look. You tell them that you don’t reward that kind of behavior.

Yet here you are, getting upset with the person behind the airline counter. Here you are, typing a rude email. Here you are, ranting on social media. Here you are, throwing the TV remote across the room.
Get over it. It happened. As we’ve said, the only thing that will make a difference is getting to work.
